intro: Martial arts and combat sports in Illinois happen in real rooms. Some are storefronts in strip malls with a dojo or dojang sign. Some are high school wrestling rooms down a hallway. Others are boxing gyms, college judo clubs and park district field houses. Each room has its own name, its own rule book and its own way of paying the rent.

In this unit you will visit those rooms through their history. You will trace words like dojo, dojang and kwoon back to Japan, Korea and Guangdong. You will meet the Chicago Tribune's Golden Gloves, the 1905 South Park field houses, Hull-House and the IHSA state wrestling series. You will see when doors opened to girls and women, and which laws helped.

By the end, you will be able to compare two training rooms. You will name who writes each room's rules, who pays for it and who could walk in, with dates. You will also read a trophy, bracket or program as a historian reads an artifact.
bigQuestion: Who built the rooms where Illinois young people box, wrestle and train, and who decided the rules inside them?

title: Illinois Storefronts

chapters.title: Four Rooms in One County
chapters.bigQuestion: What can the name, the rules and the rent of a training room tell us about where a martial art came from?

story.title: Four Doors on One Strip
story.kicker: A family looking for an after-school class finds four signs with four words for school.
paragraphs: Maya rides in the back seat along a busy road in an Illinois county. Her family is looking for an after-school class. They pull into a row of shops with one long parking lot. There is a pizza place, a phone store and a laundromat. Between them are four doors with sports signs.

The first sign says Karate Dojo. The second says Taekwondo Dojang. The third says Boxing Gym in big red letters. The fourth says Judo Club, with a small picture of a white jacket. Maya reads them out loud. "Why does every one use a different word for school?" she asks.

Her mother points at the windows. Inside the dojo, students in white line up by belt color. Inside the dojang, the flag of South Korea hangs beside the flag of the United States. Inside the gym, a square ring with ropes fills the back half of the room.

Maya's older brother wrestles for the high school. His room has no sign on any street. It sits down a hallway past the cafeteria, with mats from wall to wall and a list of weight classes taped by the door. "That makes five rooms," he says. "And each one answers to a different rule book."
story.think: Why might four schools on one strip choose four different words for the same idea?

lessons.title: Dojo: Place of the Way
lessons.mainIdea: Dojo is a Japanese word for a training hall, and it first named a place of Buddhist practice.
reading: The Japanese word *dojo* is written with two characters. The first means "way" or "path." The second means "place." So a dojo is a "place of the way." The same first character appears in judo, "the gentle way," and in kendo, "the way of the sword."

The word is older than any sport. Buddhist writers in China and Japan used it for the spot where the Buddha reached awakening. Later it named temple halls used for meditation and study. Over the centuries, Japanese sword and archery schools also called their training halls dojo.

In 1882, Kanō Jigorō opened his judo school at Eishō-ji. It was a Buddhist temple in Tokyo. He named it the *Kodokan*, meaning a hall for teaching the way. An Illinois storefront with a dojo sign borrows that long history.

words.d: a Japanese word for a training hall; it means "place of the way"
the judo school Kanō Jigorō founded in Tokyo in 1882; still the world center of judo

look.title: A Sign in Two Languages
look.text: Picture a storefront window. Large English letters read "Karate Dojo." Below them, two Japanese characters are painted in black. A newer sign next door reads "Martial Arts Academy" with no Japanese words at all.
look.prompt: What might each owner want families to understand from the sign they chose?

check.q: What does the Japanese word dojo mean, part by part?
check.why: Dojo joins the characters for way and place, so it means place of the way.

choices: at Eishō-ji, a Buddhist temple in Tokyo
check.why: The Kodokan began in a small space at the Eishō-ji temple in Tokyo in 1882.

check.q: Before sports used it, what did the word dojo name?
check.why: Buddhist writers used dojo for the place of the Buddha's awakening and later for temple halls.

lessons.title: Dojang and Gymnasium
lessons.mainIdea: Dojang is the Korean word for a training hall, and gym comes from an ancient Greek word.
reading: A taekwondo school often calls itself a *dojang*. That is the Korean word for a training hall. It is written with the same two Chinese characters as the Japanese word dojo, read the Korean way. The name taekwondo itself was chosen in South Korea in the mid-1950s.

The world headquarters of taekwondo is the *Kukkiwon* in Seoul, South Korea. It opened in 1972. The Kukkiwon issues black belt certificates to students in many countries. Many U.S. dojangs were opened by Korean immigrants who arrived after the Immigration and Nationality Act of 1965 widened entry from Asia.

The word gym is short for *gymnasium*. It comes from the ancient Greek gymnasion, a public place for exercise and study. Its root, gymnos, meant "unclothed," because Greek athletes trained that way. A boxing gym in Illinois carries a name about 2,500 years old.

words.d: the Korean word for a training hall, used by taekwondo schools
the world headquarters of taekwondo in Seoul, South Korea, opened in 1972
a room or building for exercise; from the ancient Greek gymnasion

look.title: Two Flags on a Wall
look.text: In many U.S. taekwondo schools, the flag of South Korea hangs next to the flag of the United States. Ranks are named in Korean. The students come from many backgrounds, and most of them speak English at home.
look.prompt: What does this wall tell a visitor about where the art came from and where it lives now?

check.q: What is a dojang?
choices: the Korean word for a training hall
check.why: Dojang is the Korean word for a training hall, used in taekwondo.

check.q: When did the Kukkiwon open in Seoul?
check.why: The Kukkiwon, the world headquarters of taekwondo, opened in 1972.

check.q: Where does the word gym come from?
choices: an Old English word for rope
check.why: Gym is short for gymnasium, from the Greek gymnasion.

lessons.title: Kwoon, Club and Academy
lessons.mainIdea: Chinese martial arts schools often use the Cantonese word kwoon, while other schools choose club or academy.
reading: Many Chinese martial arts schools in North America call themselves a *kwoon*. Kwoon is the Cantonese way to say guan, a word for a hall or building. Cantonese is spoken in Guangdong province and Hong Kong. Most early Chinese immigrants to the United States came from Guangdong, so Cantonese words spread first.

Bruce Lee was born in San Francisco in 1940 and grew up in Hong Kong. He came back to the United States as a young man and taught in the 1960s. He opened schools in Seattle and Oakland. Chinese American teachers in many cities ran schools long before and after him.

Other schools use words from Europe. A *club* is a group run by its members, often with dues and elected officers. The Budokwai in London, founded in 1918, is one of the oldest judo clubs in Europe. Many Brazilian jiu-jitsu schools use academia, the Portuguese word for academy.

words.d: the Cantonese word for a hall; used by many Chinese martial arts schools
a group run by its own members, who usually pay dues and elect leaders

lessons.title: The School Wrestling Room
lessons.mainIdea: A high school wrestling room is a public school space run under a state association and a national rule book.
reading: Most Illinois high schools with a team have a *wrestling room*. It is often a plain room covered wall to wall with padded mats. Public money helps build and run it, and any enrolled student may try out. The team competes in *folkstyle* wrestling, the style used in U.S. high schools and colleges.

Folkstyle differs from the two Olympic styles, freestyle and Greco-Roman. Each style has its own scoring rules. U.S. college wrestlers held their first NCAA championships in 1928. Illinois high school boys held their first state championships in 1937, run by the Illinois High School Association, or IHSA.

The rules come from the National Federation of State High School Associations, known as the *NFHS*. It was founded in Chicago in 1920. Its wrestling rule book sets the weight classes, match length and uniforms. In high school wrestling, the heaviest weight class tops out at 285 pounds.

words.d: a school room covered with mats where a wrestling team trains
the style of wrestling used in U.S. high schools and colleges
the National Federation of State High School Associations; it writes rule books for high school sports

look.title: The High School Rule Book
look.text: The book lists the weight classes, the size of the mat, what wrestlers wear, how long a match lasts and how referees award points. State associations that belong to the NFHS use it for their high school meets.
look.cite: NFHS Wrestling Rules Book, published each season by the National Federation of State High School Associations
look.prompt: Why would high schools across the country want to share one rule book?

check.why: The NFHS was founded in Chicago in 1920.

check.q: When did Illinois high school boys hold their first state wrestling championships?
check.why: The IHSA crowned its first boys state wrestling champions in 1937.

lessons.title: Karate in a Storefront
lessons.mainIdea: Karate came to U.S. storefronts after World War II, often carried home by veterans who had served in Asia.
reading: Karate grew on Okinawa, once the center of the *Ryukyu Kingdom*. Japan made the islands a prefecture in 1879. In the early 1900s, Okinawan teachers brought karate into local schools and then to mainland Japan. Funakoshi Gichin gave a well-known demonstration in Tokyo in 1922.

After World War II, U.S. troops were stationed on Okinawa and in Japan. Some trained in local karate halls. When they came home, a few opened schools of their own. Robert Trias, a Navy veteran, opened a karate school in Phoenix, Arizona, in 1946; it is often named as the first on the U.S. mainland.

Many karate schools rent a *storefront*, a shop with a window on a street or strip mall. The owner pays rent and charges monthly *tuition*, a fee for classes. The IHSA does not run karate. Each Illinois karate school follows its style's organization or sets its own ranks and rules.

words.d: the island kingdom centered on Okinawa, made part of Japan in 1879
a rented shop with a window facing a street or parking lot
a fee paid for classes

look.title: Reading a Shop Window
look.text: A storefront window shows a class schedule: young children at 4:30, teens at 5:30, adults at 7:00. A poster announces a belt test on Saturday. A sign says the first class is free. Taped low on the glass is a photo of the school's founder beside his own teacher.
look.prompt: What does this window tell you about how a storefront school pays its rent and shows where it came from?

check.q: Where did karate grow before it reached mainland Japan?
choices: Okinawa, in the old Ryukyu Kingdom
check.why: Karate grew on Okinawa, the center of the Ryukyu Kingdom.

check.q: When did Japan make the Ryukyu Islands a prefecture?
check.why: Japan made the islands Okinawa Prefecture in 1879.

check.q: What does a storefront school charge for classes?
check.why: Storefront schools charge tuition, a fee for classes, to pay rent and teachers.

lessons.title: Judo on a College Campus
lessons.mainIdea: College judo in the U.S. grew in student clubs, with San Jose State as a well-known center.
reading: Kanō Jigorō was an educator who wanted judo taught in schools. Japanese immigrants started judo clubs in Hawaii and on the U.S. West Coast in the early 1900s. Some clubs met in community halls or Buddhist temples. They taught children of the community and later welcomed others.

During World War II, the U.S. government forced about 120,000 Japanese Americans into camps. This *incarceration* closed many West Coast judo clubs. At San Jose State in California, Yosh Uchida had begun coaching judo in 1940, while still a student. After the war he built the school into a top college judo program.

Judo joined the Olympics at Tokyo in 1964. Uchida coached the first U.S. Olympic judo team there. At most U.S. colleges, judo is a *club sport*. Students run the club and pay dues, and the NCAA does not hold a judo championship.

words.d: being locked up; in U.S. history, the forced removal of Japanese Americans to camps in World War II
a college sport run by students, not by the athletic department

look.title: A Campus Flyer
look.text: A flyer on a college bulletin board reads: "Judo Club. Mondays and Thursdays, 7 p.m., Rec Center Room B. All levels welcome. Dues: $30 per semester. Officers elected each spring."
look.prompt: How can you tell from the flyer that this is a club sport and not a varsity team?

check.q: What closed many West Coast judo clubs during World War II?
choices: the forced incarceration of Japanese Americans
check.why: About 120,000 Japanese Americans were forced into camps, which closed many clubs.

check.q: Who coached the first U.S. Olympic judo team in 1964?
check.why: Yosh Uchida of San Jose State coached the first U.S. Olympic judo team.

check.q: How is judo usually run at U.S. colleges?
choices: as a club sport run by students
check.why: At most colleges, judo is a club sport; the NCAA holds no judo championship.

lessons.title: The Boxing Gym
lessons.mainIdea: A boxing gym is built around a ring, and its rules trace back to the Queensberry Rules of 1867.
reading: A boxing gym is easy to spot. A raised *ring*, a square platform with ropes, stands in the room. The name ring is older than the square shape. Early English prize fights took place inside a circle of standing spectators.

Modern boxing rules began with the *Queensberry Rules*, published in London in 1867. John Graham Chambers wrote them. They carry the name of the Marquess of Queensberry, who backed them. The rules called for padded gloves and rounds of three minutes, with one minute of rest between.

Boxing has two worlds. *Amateur* boxers are not paid; USA Boxing, based in Colorado Springs, runs their events and helps pick Olympic teams. Professional boxers fight for money. Illinois law requires professional boxers to hold a state license.

words.d: the raised square platform with ropes where a boxing match takes place
boxing rules published in London in 1867 that required gloves and timed rounds
an athlete who competes without being paid

look.title: The First Rule of 1867
look.text: Rule 1 calls for a fair stand-up boxing match in a 24-foot ring, or as near that size as can be managed.
look.cite: The Queensberry Rules, London, 1867, written by John Graham Chambers
look.prompt: What does the first rule say about the size of the space?

check.q: Who wrote the Queensberry Rules?
check.why: John Graham Chambers wrote them; the Marquess of Queensberry backed them and gave his name.

check.q: What is an amateur boxer?
choices: a boxer who has never won
a boxer with a state pro license
a boxer who competes without pay
check.why: An amateur competes without being paid; USA Boxing runs amateur events.

check.q: Why is a square boxing platform called a ring?
choices: Early prize fights took place inside a circle of spectators
The Queensberry Rules required a round floor
Rings were first used in wrestling rooms
check.why: The name is older than the square; early fights happened inside a ring of onlookers.

lessons.title: Who Writes the Rules
lessons.mainIdea: Each room on the strip answers to a different rule maker, from a state association to a world federation.
reading: The high school wrestling room follows two bodies. The NFHS writes the rule book. The IHSA, founded in 1900, runs the Illinois state series and decides which schools compete in which class. Both are groups of schools, not private businesses.

Judo answers to the *International Judo Federation*, or IJF, founded in 1951. It writes the rules used at the Olympics and world championships. In the United States, USA Judo is the national body. Taekwondo's world body began in 1973 as the World Taekwondo Federation and is now called World Taekwondo.

Karate has many rule makers. Each style, such as Shotokan or Gōjū-ryū, may have its own organizations. The World Karate Federation writes rules for sport karate, which appeared at the Tokyo Olympics held in 2021. A *governing body* is the group that makes the rules and runs the official events for a sport.

words.d: the world governing body of judo, founded in 1951
a group that makes the rules and runs official events for a sport

look.title: When the Rule Makers Began
look.cite: Founding records of the Kodokan, IHSA, NFHS, IJF, Kukkiwon and World Taekwondo
look.prompt: How many years passed between the founding of the Kodokan and the founding of the IJF?

check.q: What is a governing body?
choices: a group that makes the rules and runs official events
a person who owns a storefront
the floor of a wrestling room
check.why: A governing body makes a sport's rules and runs its official events.

check.q: When was the International Judo Federation founded?
check.why: The IJF, judo's world body, was founded in 1951.

check.q: How does karate differ from high school wrestling in who makes the rules?
choices: Karate has one world rule book and wrestling has none
Karate has many style organizations, while school wrestling follows the NFHS
Both are run by the IHSA
check.why: Karate styles have their own organizations; high school wrestling follows the NFHS rule book.

lessons.title: Belts, Records and Brackets
lessons.mainIdea: Belt arts show progress with ranks, while wrestling and boxing show it with records and tournament results.
reading: Kanō Jigorō created a ranking system for judo in the 1880s. Beginners held *kyu* grades. Advanced students earned *dan* grades, and dan holders wore a black belt. Karate teachers in mainland Japan took up the same kyu and dan system in the 1920s.

Taekwondo uses colored belts and black belt dan ranks too. A Kukkiwon certificate records a student's dan rank and can be checked in its records. Colored belts below black vary from school to school. A belt rank belongs to one art and often to one organization.

Wrestling and boxing do not use belts. A wrestler's progress shows in a *record*, the count of wins and losses, and in the state tournament bracket. A boxer also builds a record, match by match. A trophy or a medal marks a result on one day, while a belt marks a rank that stays.

words.d: a grade below black belt in judo and karate
a black belt rank; first dan is the first black belt level
the count of an athlete's wins and losses

look.title: Two Walls
look.text: In the dojo, one wall holds a row of photos of students who earned black belts, each with a date. In the high school wrestling room, one wall holds a painted list of state qualifiers and state medalists, each with a year and a weight class.
look.prompt: What does each wall honor, and how are the two kinds of honor different?

check.q: Who created the kyu and dan ranks for judo?
check.why: Kanō Jigorō created judo's kyu and dan system in the 1880s.

check.q: What is a wrestler's record?
choices: the color of the wrestler's belt
the room where the team trains
the count of wins and losses
check.why: A record counts an athlete's wins and losses.

check.q: When did karate teachers in mainland Japan take up kyu and dan ranks?
check.why: Karate adopted judo's kyu and dan system in mainland Japan in the 1920s.

lessons.title: Paying for the Room
lessons.mainIdea: Who pays for a training room shapes who can walk in, from public school budgets to monthly tuition.
reading: The high school wrestling room is paid for mostly by a public school district. Illinois school districts are funded largely by local property taxes, with state and federal money added. Students on the team do not pay tuition to use the room. Families may still pay for shoes, camps or travel.

A storefront dojo or dojang is a small business. Its owner pays rent, insurance and teachers from monthly tuition and test fees. If families stop paying, the school closes. Some storefront owners also run summer camps or after-school pickup to stay open.

Some boxing gyms are set up as *nonprofits*, organizations that put their money back into their programs. Under federal tax law, many can accept donations that givers deduct from their taxes. Public park districts, which Illinois towns fund through taxes, also host boxing and martial arts classes at low cost.

words.d: a local tax on land and buildings; it pays for much of public schooling in Illinois
an organization that uses its money for its programs, not to make owners rich

look.title: Three Price Tags
look.text: The school wrestling team asks families to buy wrestling shoes. The karate storefront charges a monthly fee plus a fee for each belt test. The park district boxing class charges a small fee for a ten-week session and offers help for families who need it.
look.prompt: Which room is easiest for a new family to try, and what paid for that room?

check.q: What pays for most of a public high school wrestling room in Illinois?
choices: public school funds, largely from property taxes
check.why: Illinois school districts are funded largely by local property taxes, with state and federal help.

check.q: What is a nonprofit?
choices: a group that uses its money for its programs
a business that never charges fees
a school run by the IHSA
check.why: A nonprofit puts its money back into its programs instead of paying owners a profit.

check.q: What happens to a storefront school if families stop paying tuition?
choices: it cannot pay rent and may close
check.why: A storefront is a small business that depends on tuition to pay rent and teachers.

lessons.title: Who Could Walk In
lessons.mainIdea: The doors of these rooms opened to women and to athletes with disabilities over many decades, often after long campaigns.
reading: In 1959, Rena "Rusty" Kanokogi of Brooklyn, New York, won a YMCA judo tournament. Officials took her medal away because she was a woman. She spent the next decades pushing for women's judo. The first women's world judo championships were held in New York in 1980.

Women's judo became an Olympic medal sport at Barcelona in 1992. Women's taekwondo arrived with the sport's first medal events at Sydney in 2000. Women's freestyle wrestling followed in 2004 at Athens. Women's boxing joined at London in 2012.

Judo entered the *Paralympic Games* at Seoul in 1988 for athletes who are blind or have low vision. Women's events were added in 2004. The Paralympics are held in the same city as the Olympics, soon after them. Each step opened a room that had been closed to someone.

words.d: the international games for athletes with disabilities, held after each Olympics
an event where Olympic medals are awarded, not just a demonstration

look.cite: International Olympic Committee, official results of the 1992, 2000, 2004 and 2012 Games

check.why: Officials took back her medal because she was a woman, and she then campaigned for women's judo.

check.why: Women's boxing first appeared as an Olympic medal event at London in 2012.

check.q: When did judo enter the Paralympic Games?
check.why: Judo joined the Paralympics at Seoul in 1988 for athletes who are blind or have low vision.

review.why: A storefront is a small business paid for by tuition and fees.

chapters.title: Chicago Gloves and Illinois Mats
chapters.bigQuestion: How did newspapers, park districts and a state school association build rooms for combat sports in Chicago and Illinois?

story.title: One Glass Case, Two Rule Books
story.kicker: A wrestling bracket and a Golden Gloves program sit side by side behind the same glass.
paragraphs: A Chicago high school has a long glass trophy case outside its gym. Most shelves hold basketball and track trophies. On the bottom shelf sit two faded pieces of paper. One is a state wrestling bracket from the IHSA finals. The other is a program from the Chicago Golden Gloves boxing tournament.

A student named Darius stops to look during passing period. The bracket has lines that join names, round by round, down to one champion at each weight. One name is circled in pen. It belongs to a wrestler who graduated from the school decades ago.

The Golden Gloves program is thinner. Its cover shows a small gold boxing glove. Inside are lists of boxers by weight class, with the names of the parks and gyms they trained in. One of those names is the same field house where Darius plays basketball on Saturdays.

Darius's history teacher walks by and sees him reading. "Those two papers came from two different rule books," she says. "One tournament was run by a state association of schools. The other was started with help from a newspaper." Darius looks again at the gold glove.
story.think: Why would a school keep papers from two different sports and two different organizations in the same case?

lessons.title: Gloves Made of Gold
lessons.mainIdea: The Golden Gloves is an amateur boxing tournament that big-city newspapers helped start in the late 1920s.
reading: The *Golden Gloves* is a tournament for amateur boxers. The New York Daily News ran a Golden Gloves tournament starting in 1927. By the late 1920s, the Chicago Tribune ran a Golden Gloves tournament in Chicago as well. Both papers printed the entry forms, the brackets and the results.

A champion in each weight class wins a small gold charm shaped like a boxing glove. That prize gave the tournament its name. Boxers are grouped by weight so that each match pairs people of similar size. Many local tournaments also split entrants into *novice* and open divisions, so beginners meet other beginners.

The Golden Gloves drew young boxers from Chicago's neighborhoods, parks and settlement houses. It was a way to compete in a large arena without turning professional. Winners in Chicago could go on to meet winners from other cities. The tournament still runs in Chicago today.

words.d: an amateur boxing tournament started with newspaper support in the late 1920s; champions win a small gold glove
a beginner; in boxing, a division for boxers with few past bouts

look.title: A Program Page
look.text: A page from an old Golden Gloves program lists boxers under headings by weight. Next to each name is a park, a gym or a club. A box at the bottom lists the tournament rules: amateur boxers only, and every boxer weighs in on the day of the bout.
look.prompt: What can a historian learn about a city's neighborhoods from the names of the gyms and parks on this page?

check.q: What does a Golden Gloves champion receive?
choices: a small gold charm shaped like a boxing glove
a college scholarship from the NCAA
check.why: Champions win a small gold glove charm, which gave the tournament its name.

check.q: Which Chicago newspaper ran the city's Golden Gloves tournament?
check.why: The Chicago Tribune ran the Chicago Golden Gloves; the New York Daily News ran New York's.

check.q: What is a novice division?
choices: a division for the heaviest boxers
a division for boxers with few past bouts
check.why: A novice division lets beginners meet other beginners.

lessons.title: A Newspaper as Promoter
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago Tribune sports editor Arch Ward used his paper to build big public sports events, including the first baseball All-Star Game.
reading: In the early 1900s, newspapers were a main source of sports news. A paper that ran its own event could fill its sports pages for weeks. It could also sell more copies. A *promoter* is a person or group that organizes an event and draws a crowd to it.

*Arch Ward* became sports editor of the Chicago Tribune in 1930 and held the job until his death in 1955. He backed the Tribune's Golden Gloves. In 1933 he created baseball's first All-Star Game, played at Comiskey Park during Chicago's Century of Progress world's fair.

In 1934, Ward started the College All-Star Game in football, played at Soldier Field. Both games drew large crowds and weeks of Tribune stories. Ward showed that a newspaper could be more than a reporter of sports. It could also be the organizer.

words.d: a person or group that organizes an event and draws a crowd to it
Chicago Tribune sports editor from 1930 to 1955 who organized big public sports events

look.title: Reporter and Organizer
look.text: Imagine the Tribune sports page in the week of the Golden Gloves finals. It prints the bracket, photos of the boxers, the ticket prices and a story praising the tournament. The paper is also the group running the tournament.
look.prompt: What might be good about a newspaper running an event? What might be a problem when it also reports on that event?

check.q: What is a promoter?
choices: a person or group that organizes an event and draws a crowd
a boxer who has turned professional
check.why: A promoter organizes an event and draws people to it.

check.q: What event did Arch Ward create in 1933?
check.why: Ward created baseball's first All-Star Game, played at Comiskey Park in 1933.

check.q: Why did newspapers like the Tribune run their own sports events?
choices: to fill their sports pages and sell more copies
check.why: An event the paper ran gave it weeks of stories and helped sell papers.

lessons.title: From City Ring to Olympic Ring
lessons.mainIdea: Amateur tournaments like the Golden Gloves fed a path that led toward national titles and the Olympic Games.
reading: Boxing first appeared at the modern Olympics in 1904, at St. Louis, Missouri. Only American boxers entered that year. Olympic boxing has been for amateurs for most of its history. That made amateur tournaments the first step toward an Olympic team.

By the 1930s, Golden Gloves champions from Chicago and New York met each year in an *Intercity* tournament. Later, a national Golden Gloves tournament brought together champions from many cities. A local win could lead to a national title and to Olympic trials.

For decades, the Amateur Athletic Union, or AAU, governed many U.S. amateur sports, including boxing. The *Amateur Sports Act of 1978* changed that. It required each Olympic sport to have its own national governing body. For amateur boxing, that body is now USA Boxing.

words.d: a Golden Gloves tournament between champions of Chicago and New York
a U.S. law that gave each Olympic sport its own national governing body

check.why: Boxing first appeared at the 1904 Olympics in St. Louis, Missouri.

check.q: What did the Amateur Sports Act of 1978 require?
choices: that each Olympic sport have its own national governing body
check.why: The 1978 law gave each Olympic sport its own national governing body.

check.q: Which two cities met in the Intercity Golden Gloves?
check.why: Intercity matches paired Golden Gloves champions from Chicago and New York.

lessons.title: Field Houses for Neighborhoods
lessons.mainIdea: In 1905, Chicago's South Park Commission opened neighborhood parks with field houses that gave crowded areas indoor public rooms.
reading: In the early 1900s, many Chicago workers lived in crowded neighborhoods near the stockyards, rail yards and factories. Few homes had space for sports. Reformers argued that small parks close to homes would help families. In 1905, the South Park Commission opened a set of new neighborhood parks on the South Side.

Each new park had a *field house*, a public building for indoor activities. The field houses were designed by the firm of D. H. Burnham and Company. The Olmsted Brothers firm designed the grounds. Inside were gymnasiums, locker rooms, showers, club rooms and, in many, a branch of the Chicago Public Library.

A field house gym was a public room. Anyone in the neighborhood could use it, not only those who paid tuition. Over the century, these rooms hosted basketball, dances, meetings, and boxing and martial arts classes. Several field houses from 1905 still stand and are city landmarks.

words.d: a public park building with a gym and rooms for indoor activities
the board that ran parks on Chicago's South Side before 1934

look.title: Two Doors
look.text: One door is on a park field house built in 1905. A sign lists free open gym hours and a low-cost boxing class for teens. The other door is a storefront karate school a few blocks away. Its sign lists monthly tuition.
look.prompt: Who might walk through each door? What paid for each room?

check.q: What is a field house?
choices: a public park building with a gym and rooms for indoor activities
check.why: A field house is a public park building with a gym and meeting rooms.

check.q: When did the South Park Commission open its new neighborhood parks?
check.why: The South Park Commission opened its new neighborhood parks with field houses in 1905.

check.q: Which firm designed the 1905 field houses?
check.why: D. H. Burnham and Company designed the buildings; the Olmsted Brothers designed the grounds.

lessons.title: One Park District
lessons.mainIdea: In 1934, Chicago joined its separate park boards into one Chicago Park District, which still runs public rooms across the city.
reading: Before 1934, Chicago had 22 separate park districts. Each had its own board, taxes and staff. The Great Depression made it hard for the small districts to pay their debts. Voters approved joining them into one body, the *Chicago Park District*, in 1934.

The new district took over parks, beaches, field houses and Soldier Field. Today it runs hundreds of parks across the city. It is a unit of local *government*, with a board and a budget funded mostly by property taxes. Its programs are open to all city residents.

Park district rooms have hosted boxing for generations. Programs at some field houses train young boxers who enter the Chicago Golden Gloves. Other parks offer martial arts classes. A park district class can reach children whose families could not pay storefront tuition.

words.d: the city park agency formed in 1934 by joining 22 separate park districts
the public bodies that make laws, collect taxes and run services

look.title: One Agency for One City
look.text: Before 1934, a family on the North Side and a family on the South Side paid taxes to different park boards. Each board had its own staff and its own debts. After 1934, one Chicago Park District board set programs and budgets for parks across the whole city.
look.prompt: Why might one citywide park agency be easier to run than 22 small ones?

check.q: How many park districts were joined to form the Chicago Park District?
check.why: Chicago's 22 separate park districts were joined in 1934.

check.q: What problem helped push Chicago to join its park districts in 1934?
choices: the Great Depression made debts hard to pay
check.why: During the Great Depression the small districts struggled to pay their debts.

check.q: How can a park district boxing class help a family?
choices: It can cost less than storefront tuition because taxes help pay for it
It is run by a newspaper
check.why: Park programs are funded mostly by taxes, so they can charge low fees.

lessons.title: A Settlement Gym and a Stadium
lessons.mainIdea: Hull-House and Soldier Field show two kinds of Chicago rooms: a neighborhood gym and a giant public stadium.
reading: Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr opened *Hull-House* on Halsted Street in 1889. It was a *settlement house*, a center where reformers lived among immigrant neighbors and offered classes and services. The Near West Side around it was home to Italian, Greek, Jewish and many other families. In the 1890s, Hull-House added a gymnasium.

Soldier Field opened in 1924 on the lakefront. On September 22, 1927, it held the heavyweight rematch between Gene Tunney and Jack Dempsey. More than 100,000 people came. Tunney won by decision, and the bout is remembered for the "long count" after a knockdown in the seventh round.

The two rooms show two sides of the city's combat sports. A settlement gym gave neighbors a free, small space to exercise and learn. A stadium sold tickets to a huge crowd to watch two professionals. Both were Chicago public history.

words.d: the settlement house founded by Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr in Chicago in 1889
a neighborhood center where reformers lived and offered classes and services to immigrants

look.cite: Hull-House records; Chicago Park District history; Chicago Tribune, September 1927

choices: Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr
check.why: Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr founded Hull-House on Halsted Street.

check.q: Which famous bout took place at Soldier Field in 1927?
check.why: Gene Tunney beat Jack Dempsey there on September 22, 1927, before more than 100,000 people.

check.q: What is a settlement house?
choices: a neighborhood center where reformers lived and served immigrants
check.why: Settlement houses like Hull-House offered classes and services to immigrant neighbors.

lessons.title: An Association of Schools
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA, founded in 1900, runs Illinois high school state tournaments, and Illinois helped found the national NFHS in 1920.
reading: The *Illinois High School Association*, or IHSA, was founded in 1900. Its headquarters is in Bloomington, Illinois. It is an association of member high schools. The schools agree on eligibility rules, such as grades and age, and the IHSA runs the state tournaments.

In 1920, leaders from Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Michigan and Wisconsin met in Chicago. They formed the Midwest Federation of State High School Athletic Associations. It grew into the national NFHS, which moved its headquarters to Indianapolis. Illinois was one of its five founding states.

The NFHS writes national rule books for many high school sports, including wrestling. The IHSA uses those rules and adds its own for Illinois, such as how schools are split into classes by enrollment. An *association* is a group whose members join together to make shared rules.

words.d: the IHSA; founded in 1900, it runs Illinois high school state tournaments
a group whose members join together to make shared rules
the rules about who is allowed to compete, such as grades and age

look.title: Two Layers of Rules
look.text: A wrestling coach keeps two books on her desk. One is the national NFHS wrestling rule book. The other is the IHSA's Illinois wrestling handbook, with dates for regionals and sectionals and the list of schools in each class.
look.prompt: Why does the coach need both books? What does each one decide?

check.q: Where is the IHSA's headquarters?
check.why: The IHSA is headquartered in Bloomington, Illinois.

check.q: Which five states founded the group that became the NFHS in 1920?
choices: Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Michigan and Wisconsin
New York, Ohio, Texas, Florida and California
Illinois, Missouri, Kansas, Nebraska and Ohio
Iowa, Minnesota, Oklahoma, Colorado and Utah
check.why: Leaders from Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Michigan and Wisconsin met in Chicago in 1920.

check.q: What does eligibility mean?
choices: the rules about who may compete, such as grades and age
check.why: Eligibility rules decide who is allowed to compete.

lessons.title: Boys' State Finals Since 1937
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois boys have wrestled for IHSA state titles since 1937, through a series of tournaments that ends in a state final bracket.
reading: The IHSA crowned its first boys state wrestling champions in 1937. That was more than 35 years after the IHSA began. Each season ends with a *state series*: regional tournaments, then sectionals, then the state finals. Wrestlers who place high enough move on to the next round.

At each level, wrestlers are listed on a *bracket*, a chart that pairs them and shows who advances. Each weight class has its own bracket. The IHSA also splits schools into classes by enrollment, so small schools compete with small schools and large schools with large schools.

For many years, the individual state finals have been held at the University of Illinois arena in Champaign. The IHSA keeps a record book with every state champion by year, weight and school. That book is a primary source for the history of Illinois wrestling.

words.d: the chain of tournaments, from regionals to state finals, that decides state champions
a chart that pairs competitors and shows who moves on
a record made at the time, such as a bracket, program or record book

look.title: Reading a Bracket
look.text: A state finals bracket for one weight class starts with sixteen names on the left side. Lines join pairs of names. Each line leads to a single name in the next column. By the far right, one name stands alone as champion, with the year and the school printed beside it.
look.prompt: What can the bracket tell you about how many wrestlers one champion had to meet?

check.q: What is a bracket?
choices: a chart that pairs competitors and shows who moves on
check.why: A bracket pairs competitors and shows who advances toward a champion.

check.q: In what order does the IHSA state series run?
check.why: The series goes from regionals to sectionals to the state finals.

check.q: Why is the IHSA record book a primary source?
choices: It records champions made at the time, year by year
It was written by a novelist
It is the NFHS rule book
check.why: A record made at the time, like a list of champions, is a primary source.

lessons.title: Girls Get Their Own Bracket
lessons.mainIdea: Illinois held its first girls state wrestling finals in 2022, fifty years after Title IX barred sex discrimination in school programs.
reading: In 1972, Congress passed *Title IX* of the Education Amendments. It bans discrimination based on sex in any education program that gets federal money. High school sports count as education programs. Title IX opened many girls teams across the country.

Combat sports moved slowly. For decades, girls who wanted to wrestle in Illinois high schools joined boys teams and wrestled boys. Their numbers grew over many years. Other states started separate girls tournaments before Illinois did.

The IHSA held its first girls state wrestling finals in 2022, at the end of the 2021–22 season. Girls now have their own weight classes and their own state bracket. The first girls champions joined the IHSA record book, eighty-five years after the first boys champions.

words.d: a 1972 U.S. law that bans sex discrimination in education programs that get federal money
treating people unfairly because of who they are, such as their sex or race

look.title: The Words of Title IX
look.text: No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.
look.cite: Title IX, Education Amendments of 1972, 20 U.S.C. § 1681
look.prompt: Which words in the law could a girl use to ask for a place on a school team?

check.q: When did Congress pass Title IX?
check.why: Title IX is part of the Education Amendments of 1972.

check.q: Before 2022, how did most Illinois girls wrestle in high school?
choices: They could not wrestle at all by law
They joined boys teams and wrestled boys
They wrestled only in Golden Gloves
check.why: Girls joined boys teams and wrestled boys until the IHSA added girls state finals.

check.q: How many years passed between the first IHSA boys and girls wrestling champions?
check.why: The first boys champions were crowned in 1937 and the first girls champions in 2022: 85 years.

lessons.title: Many Rule Books, One Case
lessons.mainIdea: Each trophy in a school case was won under a different rule book written by a different body.
reading: A school trophy case looks like one collection. Each object in it, though, comes from its own set of rules. A wrestling plaque was won under the NFHS rule book, in a state series run by the IHSA. A basketball trophy was also won under NFHS rules, but in a different sport with different officials.

A Golden Gloves program comes from outside the school. The bouts followed amateur boxing rules set by USA Boxing and the tournament's organizers. A judo medal from a local tournament followed rules shaped by the International Judo Federation. The school simply chose to display it.

Historians call an object like a trophy or program an *artifact*. An artifact is made by people and survives from the past. Reading an artifact means asking who made it, under what rules, and for whom. A single glass case can hold artifacts from four or five different governing bodies.

words.d: an object made by people that survives from the past
to show objects so that people can see them, as in a trophy case

look.title: Labels in the Case
look.text: Four objects sit on one shelf. A wooden plaque says IHSA State Wrestling, Third Place. A small gold glove hangs from a ribbon. A bronze medal is stamped with a judo club's name. A basketball rests on a stand signed by a whole team.
look.prompt: For each object, which organization's rules do you think it was won under?

check.q: What is an artifact?
choices: an object made by people that survives from the past
check.why: An artifact is a human-made object from the past, such as a trophy or program.

check.q: Which body writes the rules a high school wrestling plaque was won under?
check.why: High school wrestling follows the NFHS rule book, with the IHSA running the state series.

check.q: What rules did bouts in a Golden Gloves tournament follow?
check.why: Golden Gloves bouts follow amateur boxing rules.

lessons.title: Records That Keep Names
lessons.mainIdea: Record books, brackets and programs keep the names of athletes and let historians trace who could compete and when.
reading: Each organization keeps its own *records*. The IHSA lists state wrestling champions by year and school. Golden Gloves programs and newspaper pages list boxers by weight and gym. These papers survive in school offices, family boxes and library *archives*.

Historians use such records to answer questions. When do girls' names first appear in state results? Which neighborhoods sent boxers to the Golden Gloves in the 1930s? Which schools won titles in the first years after 1937? Each answer depends on a record kept at the time.

Records also show gaps. A list of champions from 1937 to 2021 has no girls bracket, because none existed. A missing name can be as important as a printed one. Reading records carefully helps explain whose stories were saved and whose were left out.

words.d: written lists or papers kept by an organization, such as champions by year
places where old records and papers are kept for study

look.title: A Visit to the Archive
look.text: At a library archive, a student opens a box of old Tribune sports pages from the 1930s. One page lists Golden Gloves winners by weight, with the park or gym beside each name. Another page, from the same week, lists state high school wrestling results by school.
look.prompt: What question about Chicago or Illinois history could you answer with these two pages?

check.q: What does the IHSA record book list for wrestling?
choices: state champions by year and school
check.why: The IHSA record book lists state champions by year, weight and school.

check.q: Why does a list of Illinois champions from 1937 to 2021 have no girls bracket?
choices: No girls state bracket existed until 2022
Girls wrestled only in Golden Gloves
check.why: The IHSA held its first girls state wrestling finals in 2022.

check.q: What is an archive?
choices: a place where old records are kept for study
check.why: An archive keeps old records and papers so people can study them.
